# The Peculiar Gift of Boredom

I've been thinking lately about boredom, that strange and often-despised state of mind that modern life seems designed to eliminate. We have solutions for boredom now—infinite streams of content, notifications pinging constantly, entertainment on demand at every moment. Yet somehow boredom persists, and I wonder if we're making a mistake in trying to eradicate it entirely.

There's something peculiar about boredom that I think we've lost sight of. It's not actually the enemy we've been taught it is. In fact, I'd argue that boredom might be one of the most underrated and misunderstood mental states available to us—a kind of gift we keep trying to return unopened.

When I was a child, boredom was unavoidable. It would descend on lazy summer afternoons when I'd exhausted the entertainment options available to me. No phone in my pocket. No algorithms suggesting what I should do next. Just me, the suffocating heat, and the persistent question of what to do with myself. What I remember now, looking back across the decades, is that boredom was always temporary. It was the gateway to something else.

Sometimes I'd wander into the backyard and become fascinated by ants. I'd spend an hour—genuinely, a full hour—watching them navigate their tiny highways, rebuilding their paths after I'd destructively drawn lines through them with a stick. I wasn't entertained, exactly. But I wasn't bored anymore either. The boredom had cracked open into something deeper: observation, curiosity, a kind of meditative attention.

Other times, boredom led me to create things. I'd sketch random faces in notebooks. I'd write silly stories about my pet hamster going on space adventures. I'd rearrange my room for the hundredth time, imagining it as different places—a spaceship, a cozy cabin, a detective's office. This wasn't because these activities were particularly good. It's because they were better than the itch of boredom, and better than the paralysis of having unlimited options.

There's research now that suggests boredom actually activates the default mode network in our brains—the same network associated with creative thinking, daydreaming, and insight. When we're not focused on external stimuli, our brains don't go blank. They become more internally active. They wander. They make connections between disparate ideas. Some of our best thinking happens when we're supposedly doing nothing at all.

But we've become terrified of this state. We've been sold the idea that attention is a precious commodity and that idleness is waste. Every moment should be productive. Every moment should be entertaining. Every moment should be accounted for and optimized. This belief has colonized even our rest—we consume entertainment while eating, while exercising, while commuting. We fill the spaces between things with content. We've made boredom into a kind of enemy of the optimal life.

I think this is a catastrophic error.

There's a particular tyranny that comes from the constant availability of entertainment. It's the tyranny of choice that prevents us from making any choice at all. Last night, I had a few hours free and the entire world's entertainment at my fingertips. I spent forty minutes scrolling through options without watching anything, the pleasure centers of my brain muted by the paradox of infinite choice. Finally, I put the devices away and sat with a book I'd started weeks ago. The strange thing was that the book, which had felt "okay" before, suddenly seemed fascinating. Had it improved? No. Had I? Actually, yes. I had become less distracted, more present, more capable of sustained attention.

This is what boredom can do: it clears the space for genuine engagement.

There's also something about boredom that's almost spiritual, though I'm hesitant to use that word because it's become so loaded with new age connotations. What I mean is that boredom is one of the few states that forces us to confront ourselves. When there's nothing pulling at our attention, we're alone with our own minds. This can be uncomfortable—that's partly why we flee from it. We encounter our anxieties, our dissatisfactions, our nagging sense that something isn't quite right. But this discomfort is also honest. It's real. It's the beginning of actual change.

Some of the most important moments in my life have come after periods of boredom-forced reflection. A crushing stretch of time with nothing to do led me to finally ask myself what I actually wanted to do with my life, rather than what I thought I should do. A rainy weekend with no entertainment options led to a conversation with a friend that fundamentally changed how I understood myself. A boring commute led me to notice something about my hometown that I'd been missing for years, and that observation sparked an entirely new interest.

Modern productivity culture has made us suspicious of these periods. They seem wasteful. They seem like time not being optimized. But I think the opposite is true: some of life's most important optimizations can only happen when we stop trying to optimize every moment.

There's also a political dimension to this that interests me. The constant stream of entertainment and information serves a particular function in our culture: it pacifies. It keeps us perpetually distracted. It prevents the kind of sustained, contemplative attention that might lead to critical thinking. When you're constantly in a state of stimulation, it's harder to think deeply about difficult things. Boredom, boring as it is, creates the conditions for genuine thought about what might actually matter.

I'm not saying we should all renounce modern entertainment and go live as ascetics. That's not practical or even desirable. But I think we should reconsider our relationship with boredom. Instead of seeing it as something to eliminate at all costs, maybe we could see it as a signal. A signal that we need to do something different. Not necessarily something more entertaining—something more real.

When my kids complain of boredom, my first instinct is to suggest something they could do, some entertainment I could provide. But I've started resisting that instinct. Because boredom is theirs to solve, and in solving it themselves—sometimes by doing nothing, sometimes by finding something unexpected, sometimes just by sitting with the discomfort—they're developing something important. They're developing the capacity to be present with themselves. They're developing creativity born from necessity rather than provided by consumption.

I think about the artists and writers and inventors who came before the age of infinite distraction. Many of them spent long hours in apparent idleness. They took walks. They stared out windows. They sat in cafes and observed people. They seemed to understand, intuitively, that thinking requires space. That creation requires boredom. That some of life's best discoveries happen not when we're frantically searching for them but when we've stopped looking and have simply become open to what might arrive.

The economist John Maynard Keynes predicted in the 1930s that by the end of the twentieth century, we'd have solved the problem of scarcity and would be faced with a new challenge: what to do with all our leisure time. He thought we'd need to figure out how to enjoy ourselves, how to find meaning in activities that weren't work. What actually happened was different. We invented new forms of work. We invented new things to want. We made leisure into productivity. We couldn't actually relax if we tried, because relaxation itself became something to optimize and monetize.

But maybe the real skill we need to develop is the skill of living without constant stimulation. The skill of being bored without needing to fix it immediately. The skill of sitting with discomfort without running toward entertainment. The skill of using those empty hours not for productivity but for something stranger and more valuable: just thinking. Just being.

I notice that the moments when I feel most alive are usually moments when I'm fully present in something. Not distracted. Not half-watching while scrolling. Not waiting for the next thing while experiencing this thing. These moments happen more frequently when I've created conditions for them—when I've turned off the notifications, when I've resisted the pull toward entertainment, when I've let myself be bored for long enough that boredom transformed into something else.

And I think that's what boredom really is, if we give it a chance: a threshold. A transitional state between distraction and engagement, between the surface of life and something deeper. We've become so afraid of the threshold that we've eliminated the possibility of what lies on the other side.

So maybe it's time to make friends with boredom again. Not because boredom itself is good—it's not, by definition. But because of what boredom makes possible when we don't immediately flee from it. The thinking. The creating. The noticing. The becoming aware of what we actually want rather than what we've been told to want. The simple human capacity to be present with ourselves and with the world.

That seems like a skill worth cultivating. Even if it requires tolerating the strange discomfort of having nothing to do.

Especially then, perhaps.
